mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something we all think about, but most of us don’t like to admit—our own mortality. Chapter 3 is all about facing death head-on and learning how to truly embrace the present. Picture a mentor sitting with you, speaking honestly and gently about a subject that makes a lot of folks uneasy. He doesn’t treat death as some far-off threat. Instead, he sees it as a real part of every single life. And he’s convinced—thinking about death isn’t something dark or gloomy. In fact, it’s freeing. He remembers a time when illness swept through the city, taking lives suddenly and without warning. Some people panicked, grabbing tightly onto their routines and possessions, almost like they believed those things could keep danger away. But others found a sense of calm, simply because they’d already accepted how fragile life can be. The mentor’s big idea? If you can accept that death is inevitable, you actually start living more fully. When you see each day as a gift—not something you’re owed—your whole perspective shifts. Suddenly, the little annoyances don’t bother you as much. Grudges feel less important. And the present moment? It becomes something truly special. He even encourages his friend—just once in a while—to imagine today could be the last. Not to be afraid, but to feel grateful. When tomorrow isn’t promised, the value of today stands out. Think about it: a shared meal, sunlight on your face, a kind word from someone you care about. All those simple pleasures start to mean so much more. Of course, there’s the fear of death itself. Most of us worry about the unknown—maybe pain, or losing a sense of who we are. But the mentor sees death as just another part of nature, like all the changes we go through in life. Just as sleep brings rest, death brings an end to suffering. He shares the story of an old friend, diagnosed with a terminal illness, who chose peace over struggle. Instead of fighting reality, this friend spent his final days reflecting quietly, facing what was coming with dignity. His courage became a powerful example—reminding us that anyone can find peace, even in the face of death. There’s also this idea that being afraid of death can hold us back. Sometimes, people put off their dreams, avoid taking chances, and stick to safe routines, all in hopes of dodging the inevitable. But in doing so, they can miss out on the richness life has to offer. Letting go of that fear? It’s what sets you free to chase what really matters. The mentor’s advice is simple but powerful: Use your awareness of mortality to guide your choices. When you’re facing a tough decision, ask yourself—if time were short, what would matter most? That one question can cut through all the noise, helping you focus on what’s truly valuable.
